text: Ásta les vel. Siggi les hægt. Afi og Siggi lesa saman.
words_with_history.note_en: Lesa means “read”, but also “gather”, as in gathering berries or herbs. Here Siggi brings letters together into words. The gathering sense is a reading note, not a new production target.

grammar.title: Ég les · þú lest
grammar.rule: Ég kem · þú kemur. Ég tek · þú tekur. Ég les · þú lest · við lesum.
grammar.note_en:
The present tense describes actions now or regularly. Person identifies the speaker (ég, “I”; við, “we”), listener (þú, “you”), or someone discussed (hann, “he”). Number distinguishes one from several. The stem is the part to which an ending is attached. Strong verbs change their stem vowel in parts of their conjugation; the term does not mean an action is forceful.

Several strong verbs have i-umlaut, a change in the stem vowel, in the present singular: koma → kem, kemur (“come”), taka → tek, tekur (“take”), fara → ég fer (“I go”). Ég kem með bókina means “I come with the book”; Þú kemur með orðin means “You bring the words”. Ég tek kverið means “I take the catechism”; Þú tekur bókina means “You take the book”. Ég fer ekki frá bókinni nú means “I am not leaving the book now”. The plural returns to another stem: Við tökum bók og kver, “We take a book and a catechism”. These are verb-specific patterns; do not change every a or o to e.

Lesa, “read”, is strong but has no such vowel change here: Ég les, “I read”; þú lest, “you read”; við lesum, “we read”. Afi les, og þú lest aftur means “Grandfather reads, and you read again”. The first-person singular has no added ending; the second-person singular has -t in lest. Segja, “say”, is a -ja verb: Ég segi ekki orðið nú, “I am not saying the word now”; Þú segir það, “You say it”. The j of the dictionary form does not appear in segi or segir. Læra, “learn”, has -ir in the third-person singular: Hann lærir orðin, “He learns the words”; contrast við lærum saman, “we learn together”. Reyna belongs to the weak -ir group: Þú reynir means “You try”. Prófa belongs to the earlier -ar group: Presturinn prófar means “The priest tests”.

Vil, vill (“want”), get (“can”), veit (“know a fact”) and kann (“know how”) are learned as individual forms here; their full systems come later. Ég get ekki means “I cannot manage it”. Ég veit ekki means “I do not know”. Ásta kann að lesa means “Ásta knows how to read”. Do not put an ordinary infinitive directly after get; Icelandic normally uses a different verb form there.

Þér is formal “you” when the household addresses the priest. It takes a second-person plural verb even for one listener: Viljið þér kaffi? means “Would you like coffee?”; Hafið þér gott veður hér? means “Do you have good weather here?” Learn these polite question frames as bounded formulas. They are different from ordinary dative þér. Viljið þér vera hér í nótt? means “Would you like to stay here tonight?”

Af takes the dative: af sætinu, “off the seat”. The supplied expression af sér means “off herself” here; its pronoun is for recognition only. Fermist ekki, “is not confirmed”, is a supported religious formula; it is never a gap. Skinnin, “the skins”, and mergur, “marrow”, are supported myth vocabulary, not productive targets. Annar retains its supported role; allur occurs only as the familiar allir, “everyone”. The tables collect forms actually used in the story, and leave cells not demonstrated there empty.
